meta.note: Plain-language explanations for readers who are new to the terms. They are summaries, not the legal definitions: the instrument named under 'See' governs.

terms.def: India's general law on the processing of digital personal data. It applies to banks, NBFCs, insurers and market intermediaries like any other business, alongside their sector rules.
The rules made under the Act on notice, Consent Managers, security, breach reporting, retention, children's data, Significant Data Fiduciaries and the Board, notified on 13 November 2025.
Any data about an individual who can be identified by or in relation to it. The Act covers it when it is in digital form or digitised later.
The person who decides, alone or with others, why and how personal data is processed. A lender, insurer or broker is the Data Fiduciary for its customers' data.

A person that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary, such as a cloud provider, call centre or lending service provider. It needs a valid contract with the Data Fiduciary, which stays responsible.
The individual the data is about. For a child it includes the parent, and for a person with disability it includes the lawful guardian.

Permission that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, for a specified purpose, after a notice. It can be withdrawn as easily as it was given.
The statement a Data Fiduciary must give with or before a request for consent, listing the data, the purpose and how to withdraw consent, exercise rights and complain to the Board.
Cases in s. 7 where data may be processed without consent, such as data the person gave voluntarily for a purpose, legal duties to disclose to the State, court orders, emergencies and employment.

A company registered with the Data Protection Board that runs a platform through which people give, manage, review and withdraw consent across Data Fiduciaries. Registration opened on 13 November 2026.

Any unauthorised processing, or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data, that compromises its confidentiality, integrity or availability.
The detailed report on a personal data breach that a Data Fiduciary must send to the Board within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, after a first intimation without delay.

A Data Fiduciary, or class of them, that the Central Government notifies because of the volume and sensitivity of its data and the risks involved. It must appoint a Data Protection Officer in India and an independent auditor, and run yearly impact assessments and audits.
The individual a Significant Data Fiduciary appoints, based in India and answerable to its board, who represents it under the Act and handles grievances.
An assessment of the rights of Data Principals, the purpose of processing and the risks to their rights, which a Significant Data Fiduciary must carry out every twelve months.
The body set up on 13 November 2025 to take breach reports and complaints, inquire, direct remedial steps and impose penalties under the Act. It works as a digital office.
A commitment that a person under inquiry offers the Board and the Board accepts. It bars further proceedings on what it covers, unless it is breached.

Consent of a parent or lawful guardian that the Data Fiduciary checks against reliable identity and age details, or a token from an authorised entity such as DigiLocker, before processing a child's data.
Anyone under eighteen. Their data needs a parent's verifiable consent, and they may not be tracked, monitored or targeted with advertising.
Sending personal data outside India. The Act allows it unless the Government restricts a country by notification, and keeps stricter sector rules, such as RBI's data storage rules, in force.
An agent of a lender that does part of its digital lending, such as sourcing, servicing or recovery. RBI makes the lender responsible for the LSP's handling of borrower data.
The national agency for cyber incidents. Its 2022 directions require incidents to be reported within six hours and logs kept for 180 days in India.

Passwords, financial, health, biometric and similar information protected under the 2011 rules made under s. 43A of the IT Act. On 13 May 2027 the DPDP Act omits s. 43A and the rule-making power behind those rules, and the DPDP regime takes over.
